claims.claim: On the way to Constance John XXIII's wagon overturned on the Arlberg and he lay in the snow under it; asked if anything ailed him, he said 'I lie here in the devil's name'
Seeing Bludenz and the land below, John XXIII said 'Sic capiuntur vulpes', 'thus are foxes caught'
Lützow calls Richental a 'very entertaining, though very mendacious chronicler of the council'
Buck dates the Aulendorf codex of Richental to the mid-1400s, a copy of a lost original of the 1420s
Finke holds that Fillastre is the author of the Gesta, citing Segovia and a note in the Escorial manuscript
Mladoňovice says he wrote from what he saw and heard
Fillastre says the schism had lasted thirty years when the cardinals of both obediences called the Council of Pisa
At Pisa Benedict and Gregory were deposed and Alexander V chosen, by Fillastre's account
Mansi's acts of Pisa date the council to 1409
Despite the deposition, Spain except Portugal obeyed Benedict, and Naples, Carlo Malatesta, the dukes of Bavaria and the archbishop of Trier obeyed Gregory
Alexander V died within a year of his election and John XXIII was chosen
Sigismund asked the pope for the power to call a general council and choose its place and time; the cardinals pressed the pope
Cardinals Challant and Zabarella chose Constance and 1 November 1414 with the king's consent; at Lodi the pope called the council by bull with the king present
Fillastre's closing judgment says John XXIII fled from the council and called it 'quasi coactus'
Laurence of Březová says John XXIII called the council at Sigismund's wish and that it began on All Saints' day 1414
Prague in 1420 calls Sigismund the 'autor, patronus et rector' of the Council of Constance
On 4 July 1415 Gregory XII's cardinal Giovanni Dominici convoked and authorized the council by his master's authority
The council's aims were the peace and perfect union of the church and its reform
While the union matter lay silent the council acted against Hus and the errors of Wyclif
Fillastre: the pope entered Constance on Sunday 28 October 1414
The procession set for 3 November was halted when the pope fell ill; on Monday 5 November the procession and Mass were held 'et ita inceptum est concilium'
Cerretanus heads his register with the council begun on 1 November 1414 and says the pope's illness on 3 November came from indigestion and the opening was put off to 5 November
Fillastre puts the first session on Friday 16 November 1414
Richental's opening day reads 'the sixth day in the third autumn month, that was the Sunday before Martinmas'
The last session, XLV, met on Friday 22 April 1418, Martin V presiding, and closed with 'Domini, ite in pace'
Fillastre gives the council's length as three years, five months and twenty-two days
Fillastre left Constance on 2 April 1418 as legate to France; a manuscript note says the last decrees are missing because the writer left
Richental counts 5 patriarchs, 33 cardinals, 47 archbishops, 145 bishops, 93 assistant bishops, 132 abbots and 155 provosts, the abbots and provosts written with their names
Richental counts 37 universities, envoys of over 83 kings, and over 700 open prostitutes 'not counting the secret ones'
The total of 72,460 persons is marked by Buck as a later hand
Richental names two dukes from Greece as envoys of the emperor of Constantinople
Richental names envoys of Witold of Lithuania, the Serbian despot, Wallachia, two Turkish kings and the duke of White Rus'
The acts give two hundred fathers at session IV, a manuscript adding 'or about'
Fillastre says the French nation had four hundred persons of standing
Walsingham names the English delegation, among them the bishops of Salisbury, Bath and Hereford, the abbot of Westminster and the earl of Warwick
On 25 February 1418 Gregory, a Ruthenian archbishop of the order of St Basil, said to be metropolitan of all Rus', came before Martin V with six priests
Gregory said the emperor of Constantinople and the patriarch wanted union, by way of a council
Fillastre: fifty-three electors, with three cells kept for absent men
Glassberger: 23 cardinals and 30 men of the nations, six from each, making 53, and lists them by name
Richental: all fifty-three were in the chapel of the warehouse when the cry 'We have a pope: Oddone Colonna' went up
Haec sancta: the council has power immediately from Christ, which everyone, even the papal, must obey in what concerns the faith, the ending of the schism and reform in head and members
Mansi's session IV text prints the reform clause of Haec sancta in brackets, and a manuscript note says the article was imperfect and supplied in the next session

On 30 March Zabarella read the decrees but left out the article on the council's power in reform, holding it not true in law; on 6 April the elect of Poznań read them in full because Zabarella would not
Mansi names Andrew, elect of Poznań, as reading the constitutions in session V

Sentence of 4 May 1415 (session VIII): Wyclif a notorious heretic who died in heresy; his body and bones, if they can be told from other faithful bodies, to be dug up and cast out; no one appeared to defend him
Fillastre says the 4 May sentence was read, he objected, and it did not pass into a judgment; 266 further articles from the English
On 6 July the council condemned 45 articles of Wyclif and 260 others, approved the Roman council's sentence, and condemned his memory
Session XIII: communion of the laity under the bread alone stands, and those who stubbornly call it unlawful are to be shut out as heretics
Hus's thirty articles condemned in session XV, the first 'Unica est sancta universalis Ecclesia, quae est praedestinatorum universitas'
Hus in De Ecclesia: the church is the totality of the predestinate
The sentence of 6 July names six bishops to degrade Hus (Milan, Feltre, Asti, Alessandria, Bangor, Lavaur) and leaves him to secular judgment
Fillastre: Hus was condemned, degraded and handed to the secular court, and burned outside the city the same day
The acts name Jean de Brogny, cardinal of Ostia, presiding at session XV, with the king present in regalia
Mladoňovice says the session of 6 July was held with the king of the Romans presiding
Mladoňovice says seven bishops attended the degradation
Mladoňovice: 'Committimus animam tuam diabolo'; Hus answered, 'Et ego eam committo piissimo domino Jesu Christo'; the paper crown had three devils and 'Hic est haeresiarcha'
Hus said on 6 July that he had come freely under the king's safe-conduct, wishing to show his innocence
Hus would not recant because he would have to give up many truths and become a perjurer and a stumbling-block (letter of mid-June 1415)
Hus calls the council proud and avaricious, condemning his Czech books unseen (letter of 26 June 1415)
Hus reached Constance on Saturday 3 November 1414
Hus was arrested on the Wednesday after St Catherine's day, which Palacký glosses as 28 November
Stephen Páleč and Michael de Causis instigated the cardinals to arrest Hus
Hus wrote on 4 November that he had come without a safe-conduct; Novotný says it reached him on 5 November
The safe-conduct is dated Speyer, 18 October 1414
John of Chlum told the pope he had brought Hus under the safe-conduct of the king of the Romans
Richental says Hus hid in a hay wagon to flee and was caught
Mladoňovice says the story that Hus escaped in hay was false
Lützow rejects Richental's hay-wagon tale and reports the guess that he confused Hus with Jerome
Session XIX (23 September 1415): no safe-conduct to heretics bars a church judge, even if they came trusting it
A decree declares that Sigismund, notwithstanding the safe-conduct, did 'quod licuit et quod decuit' towards Hus (Mirbt from von der Hardt IV 521)
Fillastre: John XXIII fled after midnight on the night of Wednesday to Thursday, 21 March 1415, by water, with Frederick of Austria, to Schaffhausen
Richental: John fled on 20 March 1415 an hour after noon, on a small horse in a grey cloak and hood, with a crossbow, while Frederick jousted
Walsingham: John pretended illness and left suddenly by night
John XXIII said he left for fear of the king of the Romans
John XXIII was deposed on Wednesday 29 May 1415 and accepted the sentence
Gregory XII resigned through Carlo Malatesta on 4 July 1415
Fillastre's closing judgment: two who acted as popes were deposed, the third resigned
Benedict XIII was deposed on 26 July 1417; Fillastre composed and read the sentence
Benedict's written reply denied this could be a general council, having no cardinals or bishops; all there were schismatics and excommunicate
Richental has all three popes deposed on Corpus Christi eve 1415
Frequens (session XXXIX, 9 October 1417): councils five years after this one, then seven, then every ten years for ever
Jerome recanted on 23 September 1415, revoked it in May 1416, calling Hus a good man and saying he had abjured for fear of the fire
On Saturday 30 May 1416 Jerome was condemned, taken by the secular court and burned
Poggio dates his letter on Jerome to 30 May 1416, the day he died, and says he saw it
Poggio: Jerome stood fearless, 'ut alterum Catonem dixisses'
Richental tells Jerome's burning in his 1415 pages and again in his May 1416 pages
Session XIX (23 September 1415): a vicar general for the Observants of France, Burgundy and Touraine, Nicholas Rudolphi, by agreement with the Conventuals
Cerretanus: the electors chose Oddone Colonna on Thursday 11 November 1417, St Martin's day, and he took the name Martin V
Richental names the archbishop Jerg, 'Kyfionensis', of the Greek faith, arriving on 19 February 1418 with five bishops
The acts date session IV to Saturday 30 March 1415, the second-last day of the month; Fillastre calls it the Saturday of the Easter vigil
Fillastre names a Spanish nation, with Italian, French, German and English nations, in the election debate of October 1417
Michael de Causis posted the processes against Hus in the church the day after he arrived
Ludwig, son of Clem of Bavaria, held the golden orb and led Hus to execution at the king's word
The bishop of Lodi preached on heresy at Hus's sentence
Fillastre: at session I the cardinal of Florence read a schedule and the bull of convocation
Fillastre: the name Martin was chosen in honor of St Martin
Fillastre: 'Laudetur et benedicatur altissimus, qui dedit hec in pace fieri et ecclesiam sub uno capite constitui'
Fillastre: as the accessions were made, children in surplices sang Veni creator outside and many electors wept
Fillastre: the cardinal of Pisa went over first; Fillastre and the cardinal of Foix were among the last
Walsingham: Richard, bishop of London, first acceded to Colonna and all agreed at once
Martin V was consecrated on Sunday 21 November 1417 by the cardinal of Ostia (Fillastre)
At the last session the Polish envoys asked for the condemnation of John Falkenberg's book; Martin V said he would keep what was decreed in matters of faith 'conciliariter ... et non aliter'
Paulus Wladimiri, canon of Kraków, was among the Polish envoys at the last session
Mansi names Pavia as the place of the next council
Richental: learned men of Sweden, Denmark and Norway asked the council in a session on Candlemas eve 1415 to canonize Bridget, and she was canonized
Finke's calendar lists a Swedish envoy's sermon on St Bridget on 1 February 1415
Gerson's sermon of 23 March 1415: the church or a general council is a rule which anyone, even a pope, must hear and obey
Finke's calendar dates Gerson's 'Ambulate' sermon to 23 March 1415
Jean Petit's proposition justifying the murder of the duke of Orléans was condemned on 6 July 1415
The prior of Windesheim returned from Constance and told of Sigismund's Latin speech on unity and his visit to the cell of the author of the Horologium
The Bohemian barons wrote on 12 May 1415, 250 of them by Palacký's heading, asking for Hus's release
The nobles' letter of 2 September 1415 calls Hus 'vir utique bonus, justus et catholicus' and vows to defend the preachers of God's law 'usque effusionem sanguinis'
Palacký's heading gives 452 seals, and his note counts them across eight letters
Hus defended the communion of the cup from prison against the council
Laurence of Březová says Jakoubek of Stříbro began giving communion under both kinds in Prague in 1414
Prague, 10 July 1420: Sigismund had his legate raise 'illam impiam crucem Antichristi' and let Hus be burned 'sub suo salvo aut potius calvo conductu'
Inter cunctas (22 February 1418) condemns the articles again and asks suspects whether Constance represents the universal church
Bannwart: Rome never confirmed all of Constance's decrees; Eugene IV in 1439 rejected Haec sancta as impious and scandalous and in 1446 received Constance without prejudice to the Apostolic See
The Gallican Articles say the decrees of sessions IV and V stand unmoved and are not to be restricted to the time of schism
Bannwart notes Innocent XI rejected the Articles on 11 April 1682 and they were condemned in Inter multiplices, 4 August 1690
Luther, 1520: Hus and Jerome were burned at Constance in violation of the safe-conduct; 'I have not yet found any errors in his writings'
The 1916 editors say Luther was wrong to give Jerome a safe-conduct
Exsurge Domine condemns the claim that some of Hus's articles condemned at Constance are 'christianissimi, verissimi et evangelici'
Piccolomini: both bore death with a steady mind and hurried to the fire as if invited to a feast
Foxe heads the decree on Wyclif's bones 'A.D. 1425' and says they were burned and the ashes drowned

contested_claims.claim: The opening day of the council
contested_claims.sides: 1 November 1414, the day set: Fillastre (council-of-constance_acta-concilii-constanciensis-bd2-lat_finke1923.txt l.870), Cerretanus's heading (council-of-constance_acta-concilii-constanciensis-bd2-lat_finke1923.txt l.8689-8693), Březová (laurentius-de-brezova_historia-hussitica-lat-ces_goll1893.txt l.35704-35708). 5 November, the procession and Mass: Fillastre (council-of-constance_acta-concilii-constanciensis-bd2-lat_finke1923.txt l.923-927), Cerretanus (council-of-constance_acta-concilii-constanciensis-bd2-lat_finke1923.txt l.9317-9324), Mansi's index (mansi_sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-tomus-27-1409-1418-lat_welter-facsimile1902.txt l.530). 16 November, the first session: Fillastre (council-of-constance_acta-concilii-constanciensis-bd2-lat_finke1923.txt l.928-929). Richental's 'sixth day ... Sunday before Martinmas' (richental_chronik-des-constanzer-concils-gmh_buck1882.txt l.1721-1722).

contested_claims.claim: The day and manner of John XXIII's flight
contested_claims.sides: After midnight on the night to 21 March, by water: Fillastre (council-of-constance_acta-concilii-constanciensis-bd2-lat_finke1923.txt l.1385-1398). 20 March, an hour after noon, on horseback in disguise: Richental (richental_chronik-des-constanzer-concils-gmh_buck1882.txt l.3437-3460). By night, feigning illness: Walsingham (walsingham_historia-anglicana-v2-lat_riley1863.txt l.26600-26601).

contested_claims.claim: In which session Haec sancta was made, and what was read
contested_claims.sides: Read on 30 March (session IV) without the reform article, in full on 6 April (session V): Fillastre (council-of-constance_acta-concilii-constanciensis-bd2-lat_finke1923.txt l.1530-1572). Mansi prints the clause in brackets in session IV with a note that it was supplied in the next session (mansi_sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-tomus-27-1409-1418-lat_welter-facsimile1902.txt l.60405-60416, 60518-60524). Session V: Mirbt (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.13920). Sessions IV and V: Bannwart (denzinger_enchiridion-symbolorum-lat_bannwart1911.txt l.16212-16213) and the Gallican Articles (denzinger_enchiridion-symbolorum-lat_bannwart1911.txt l.23513).

contested_claims.claim: The binding force of Haec sancta
contested_claims.sides: Never confirmed in full by Rome, rejected by Eugene IV in 1439, received with Rome's rights reserved in 1446: Bannwart (denzinger_enchiridion-symbolorum-lat_bannwart1911.txt l.16207-16222). Approved by the Apostolic See and not limited to the time of schism: the Gallican Articles (denzinger_enchiridion-symbolorum-lat_bannwart1911.txt l.23505-23516). Martin V's 'conciliariter ... et non aliter' (mansi_sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-tomus-27-1409-1418-lat_welter-facsimile1902.txt l.129310-129315) is held, but no held writer argues it either way.

contested_claims.claim: When Wyclif was condemned, and how many further articles
contested_claims.sides: 4 May 1415, session VIII: the acts (mansi_sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-tomus-27-1409-1418-lat_welter-facsimile1902.txt l.64789, 65536-65566; denzinger_enchiridion-symbolorum-lat_bannwart1911.txt l.15776-15778). The 4 May sentence did not stand; condemnation on 6 July: Fillastre (council-of-constance_acta-concilii-constanciensis-bd2-lat_finke1923.txt l.1861-1871, 2567-2575). 266 further articles (council-of-constance_acta-concilii-constanciensis-bd2-lat_finke1923.txt l.1864) against 260 (council-of-constance_acta-concilii-constanciensis-bd2-lat_finke1923.txt l.2573).

contested_claims.claim: Whether Hus tried to escape
contested_claims.sides: Hid in a hay wagon and was caught: Richental (richental_chronik-des-constanzer-concils-gmh_buck1882.txt l.3261-3283). A false rumour: Mladoňovice (palacky_documenta-mag-joannis-hus-lat-ces_1869.txt l.13603-13619). Lützow, modern, rejects Richental's tale (lutzow_life-and-times-of-hus_1909.txt l.9435-9450).

contested_claims.claim: Who presided at Hus's sentence, and how many bishops degraded him
contested_claims.sides: Jean de Brogny, cardinal of Ostia, with the king present; six bishops named: the acts (mansi_sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-tomus-27-1409-1418-lat_welter-facsimile1902.txt l.77804-77816, 78650-78661). The king of the Romans presiding; seven bishops: Mladoňovice (palacky_documenta-mag-joannis-hus-lat-ces_1869.txt l.17086-17091, 17245-17247).

contested_claims.claim: How the three popes were removed
contested_claims.sides: John deposed 29 May 1415, Gregory resigned 4 July 1415, Benedict deposed 26 July 1417: Fillastre (council-of-constance_acta-concilii-constanciensis-bd2-lat_finke1923.txt l.2159-2168, 2412-2418, 6645-6681, 8626-8629). All three deposed on Corpus Christi eve 1415: Richental (richental_chronik-des-constanzer-concils-gmh_buck1882.txt l.3975-3983). Gregory renounced first: Walsingham (walsingham_historia-anglicana-v2-lat_riley1863.txt l.26587-26589).

contested_claims.claim: When Jerome was burned
contested_claims.sides: 30 May 1416: Fillastre (council-of-constance_acta-concilii-constanciensis-bd2-lat_finke1923.txt l.3256-3297), Poggio (palacky_documenta-mag-joannis-hus-lat-ces_1869.txt l.32737-32752). Told among Richental's 1415 events and again in May 1416 (richental_chronik-des-constanzer-concils-gmh_buck1882.txt l.4720-4757, 5194-5195).

contested_claims.claim: Who first went over to Colonna in the conclave
contested_claims.sides: The cardinal of Pisa: Fillastre (council-of-constance_acta-concilii-constanciensis-bd2-lat_finke1923.txt l.8097-8121). Richard, bishop of London: Walsingham (walsingham_historia-anglicana-v2-lat_riley1863.txt l.28073-28078).

contested_claims.claim: The safe-conduct
contested_claims.sides: Hus came under the king's safe-conduct: Hus on 6 July, by Mladoňovice (palacky_documenta-mag-joannis-hus-lat-ces_1869.txt l.17200-17204); John of Chlum (palacky_documenta-mag-joannis-hus-lat-ces_1869.txt l.13785-13790). He came without it, and it reached him on 5 November: Hus's letter and Novotný (hus_korespondence-a-dokumenty-lat-ces_novotny1920.txt l.14826-14828, 14871-14873). It did not bind against a heretic: the council (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.13959-13999). Broken: Prague in 1420 (palacky_urkundliche-beitraege-hussitenkrieg-v1-deu-lat_1873.txt l.2329-2333) and Luther (luther_works-v2-selected_jacobs-spaeth1916.txt l.4306-4309).

contested_claims.claim: Whether the council canonized Bridget of Sweden
contested_claims.sides: Canonized at a session on Candlemas eve 1415: Richental (richental_chronik-des-constanzer-concils-gmh_buck1882.txt l.3027-3058). Canonized by Boniface IX in 1391 and confirmed by John XXIII in 1414: Cumming, on her Who card (Build/Ministry/Features/Church-Family-Tree/Who-Profiles/era6/batch2/bridget-of-sweden.card.json l.46-48).

contested_claims.claim: The arrival of Gregory, the Ruthenian archbishop
contested_claims.sides: A Friday before 25 February 1418: Fillastre (council-of-constance_acta-concilii-constanciensis-bd2-lat_finke1923.txt l.8387-8390). 19 February 1418 with five bishops, naming him Jerg, archbishop 'Kyfionensis', of the Greek faith: Richental (richental_chronik-des-constanzer-concils-gmh_buck1882.txt l.7167-7171). 21 January with eight bishops, year not stated in the lines read: Richental (richental_chronik-des-constanzer-concils-gmh_buck1882.txt l.2734-2738).

absent_details.note: Not found. The held lists are Richental's narrative lists, Glassberger's electors and Mansi's swearers of the Narbonne articles (index only); searched MANSI27, FIN2 and RICH for subscription lists.

absent_details.detail: A total head-count by Richental himself
absent_details.note: The 72,460 at the end of his recapitulation is marked by Buck as a later hand (richental l.11686).

absent_details.detail: The surname of Gregory, the Ruthenian archbishop
absent_details.note: Fillastre's text gives an ellipsis after 'archiepiscopus'; searched all of cic/texts for Tsamblak, Camblak, Zamblak and Samblak with no hit.

absent_details.detail: The burning of Wyclif's bones
absent_details.note: The council ordered them dug up in 1415 (Mansi); the burning is held only in Foxe, under the heading A.D. 1425.

absent_details.detail: Wyclif's own words matched to the forty-five articles
absent_details.note: His works are held (wyclif_* files) but were not checked against the articles; the entry gives the condemned teaching as the acts state it.

absent_details.detail: Benedict XIII's own written reply
absent_details.note: Known here only through Fillastre's summary; Finke's third volume, which may hold Benedict-side texts, was not read beyond its header.

absent_details.detail: Luther at Leipzig in 1519 in his own words
absent_details.note: Not held; only a 1930 editor's introduction and Exsurge Domine, article 30. Searched for leipzig or lipsi with hus, hussit or bohem nearby.

absent_details.detail: The First Vatican Council naming Constance
absent_details.note: The held text of Pastor aeternus (Denzinger) does not name Constance; searched every CONSTANTI hit in Denzinger.

absent_details.detail: A held writer arguing what Martin V's 'conciliariter ... et non aliter' meant
absent_details.note: None found; the text is held in Mansi, but no held source argues its sense either way.

absent_details.note: Not stated in the lines read (richental l.2734-2738).

claims.claim: The Greeks reached the port of Ferrara on 7 March 1438 and spent the night aboard. The patriarch entered next morning
Bishops sent by the pope told Joseph II he must kiss the pope's foot. He asked which synod or canon granted the custom and whether the other apostles knelt to kiss Peter's feet
Joseph offered to embrace the pope as brothers do. Unless the kiss was remitted, he said, he would never step from the boat on to land
The pope gave way and received the patriarch in his chamber with only the cardinals present
In the Greek acts the patriarch kissed the cheek of the pope, who stood, and the others kissed his right hand and cheek. No quarrel is told
Petit dates the emperor's entry to Ferrara to 4 March and the patriarch's to 8 March 1438
Syropoulos was great ecclesiarch, a member of the Greek delegation, and signed the decree of union
Syropoulos's memoir is hostile to the union (its 1660 title: the true history of the untrue union)
The Greek acts are a first-person record of the delegation. Mansi does not name the writer. Petit gives him in brackets as Dorotheos of Mitylene
The main acts of Basel's sessions are not among our sources. Basel is held through quotation in Raynaldus, Glassberger, Mirbt and Mansi's appendices
Basel's acts, as Raynaldus quotes them, say John Palomar and John of Ragusa arrived on 19 July 1431. They opened the council on 23 July, by authority Martin V and Eugenius gave Cesarini
Mansi's note says that at Basel's opening no bishops were present, only a few abbots
Glassberger dates Basel's first session to Friday 7 December 1431
Glassberger says Martin V sent Cardinal Julian to begin the council at Basel. Eugenius IV confirmed him as legate, above all to root out the heresy of the Hussites
The Taborite chronicle says Basel invited the Bohemians to a free hearing. In 1433 their envoys set out the Four Articles before the whole council

Glassberger says the Basel fathers held, by the decrees of Constance renewed at Basel, that a lawful general council had power directly from Christ. It stood above the pope, and he could not move or dissolve it without its consent
Bannwart notes that Eugenius IV rejected the Constance teaching on 4 September 1439 as impious and scandalous
Bannwart notes that in 1446 Eugenius received Basel from its beginning up to the transfer he made
Bissipatus, the Greek envoy, told Basel in 1437 that the place must suit the Greeks and the pope, whose presence was needed above all
At session XXV on 7 May 1437 Basel's majority chose Basel, Avignon or a town of Savoy, Raynaldus says

Mansi's note says two opposed decrees were read on the same day in the same session. The majority, with the Cardinal of Arles, gave the Greeks Basel, Avignon or Savoy. The party with the papal legates gave Florence, Udine or another place
Raynaldus says Eugenius called the ecumenical synod with the Greeks at Ferrara by letters dated 18 September 1437 (XIV kal. Octobris)
Mansi argues the bull of transfer is dated 18 September 1437 and that the date 1 October in Justiniani's printed acts is a mistake
Glassberger says Eugenius moved the Basel council to Ferrara in consistory at Bologna, saying the Greeks had chosen that place

Ferrara's first session was held on Wednesday 8 January 1438 under the legate Nicholas Albergati (the record Raynaldus quotes). Raynaldus counts five archbishops, eighteen bishops, four bishops-elect and many heads of orders
Ferrara decreed that those staying at Basel under the name of a council, better called a conventicle, had incurred the penalties of the transfer
Eugenius's decree of 9 April 1438 declared, with the emperor and patriarch consenting, the holy ecumenical synod to be at Ferrara. Both sides answered 'We receive and approve'
The Greek acts say the synod was proclaimed by common consent for 9 April, Wednesday of Holy Week
Petit calls the opening day Tuesday of Holy Week, 9 April
The Greek acts report Eugenius saying, 'Where I am with the emperor and the patriarch, there is the whole synod of Christians'
Petit says purgatory was taken first, at private meetings from 13 April 1438, with Mark and Bessarion answering for the Greeks
Mark of Ephesus says the first public debate was on the addition to the Creed, then the doctrine at Florence
The Roman history before the acts lists the procession and Filioque, azymes, purgatory, the saints' vision and the primacy as the main questions

Eugenius's decree moved the council from Ferrara to Florence in session XVI, dated 1438 by the Incarnation (IV id. Januarii), that is 10 January 1439, with the emperor and patriarch consenting and the council approving
Raynaldus says the council was moved because the plague had not left Ferrara
Syropoulos lists the bishops of twenty sees, from Ephesus to Anchialus, and Isidore of Russia with one bishop
The Roman history says envoys of the churches of Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem were present
Syropoulos says the emperor's man brought two bishops and an envoy from Georgia. Later he speaks of one Georgian bishop and one lay prince

Doukas names Mark of Ephesus, Bessarion, Isidore, Balsamon, Gemistos of Lacedaemon, George Scholarios and Argyropoulos among the Greeks. He says Mark led for the Greeks and Cardinal Julian for the Latins
The Turks pressed the eastern empire harder every day, the Roman history says
The chronicle under Sphrantzes's name has Manuel II tell his son the Turks feared a union of Greeks and western Christians
Chalkokondyles says the pope at Ferrara asked the emperor to help him in his quarrel with the Germans
The Greek acts say the patriarch died suddenly after supper, having written in his room. They print his statement found afterwards
The statement says: everything the catholic and apostolic church of our Lord Jesus Christ of elder Rome holds and teaches, I too hold
The Greek acts date the patriarch's death at Florence to 9 June
Syropoulos dates the death to 10 June and says he died before the signing
Doukas says the patriarch died after the union. The notes to Doukas correct him, giving 10 June and the Greek signing on 5 July
Mark of Ephesus says the patriarch had long since been corrupted and followed the unionists
Syropoulos says the definition was signed on the Sunday, written half in Latin and half in Greek on one parchment
Syropoulos says 'with tears and sighs most of us signed', and that no money was asked for or promised at the signing
Syropoulos says Eugenius looked over the Greek signatures and signed standing. He asked whether Mark had signed, and on hearing he had not said, 'Then we have achieved nothing'
The Greek acts say the definition was read on Monday 6 July 1439 after Mass, in Latin by Cardinal Julian and in Greek by Bessarion
The decree opens: 'Let the heavens rejoice and the earth be glad.' Then: 'the wall that divided the western and the eastern church has been taken away'

The decree teaches that the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son as from one principle and one spiration. It reads the Greek 'through the Son' in that sense. It says the Filioque was added lawfully and with good reason
The decree allows the eucharist in unleavened or leavened wheat bread, each priest following his own church's custom. It teaches purgatory and the vision of God
The decree gives the apostolic see and the Roman pontiff primacy over the whole world. It calls the pope true vicar of Christ and head of the whole church
The Greek acts say the clause saving the patriarchs' privileges and rights was added, and the Latins tried to drop 'all'
The signed list opens with Eugenius and the cardinals. The emperor signs first on the Greek side
Our count of the printed list gives more than a hundred Latin signatures and about thirty Greek. The OCR breaks lines, so the count is approximate
Isidore signed as metropolitan of Kiev and holding the place of the patriarch of Antioch
The general of the Camaldolese (Ambrose) and the general of the Friars Minor signed
The Roman editor says many fathers left after the last session before the signing
Syropoulos says Mark kept silent at the signing and Isaias of Stauropolis slipped away from Florence when the signing began
Syropoulos says neither Georgian envoy gave his vote to the union. Both had slipped away
Doukas says all agreed except Mark
Mark says he kept his written statement back, stood apart from the others and held to his Fathers
Mark says the others were lured by promises and gifts
Syropoulos says the emperor would not let the pope judge Mark: as Mark was their bishop, judgment belonged to the Greeks
Basel's session XXXIII issued three propositions on 16 or 17 May 1439, which Raynaldus calls false
Basel's session XXXIV, on 25 June 1439 (VII kal. Julii), tried to depose Eugenius
Raynaldus says only seven bishops took part in the deposition. Aeneas Silvius, as he quotes him, says no Aragonese or Spanish prelate came, and from Italy only the bishop of Grosseto and an abbot
On 4 September 1439 at Florence the decree Moyses condemned Basel's teaching and the attempt to depose the pope
Glassberger says Basel defined the Immaculate Conception. His editors say the definition never bound the faith, since it was not the act of a lawful council
Glassberger says Basel's electors chose Amadeus, duke of Savoy, as Felix V on 17 November 1439, and the schism lasted to 1448
Mansi's note says the Basel party moved to Lausanne and held its first session there on 24 July 1448. Felix gave up his title on 7 April 1449
The Lausanne synod's decree is dated 16 April 1449. It says the synod, while lawfully gathered at Basel, had not consented when Eugenius set up a meeting at Ferrara under a council's name
The French envoys' instrument dated at Lausanne on 4 April 1449 speaks of Pope Nicholas's wish for peace and union
In 1516 the Fifth Lateran Council called Basel after the transfer a little council, or rather a gathering, no longer deserving the name of council
The Armenian decree Exultate Deo is dated in a public session at Florence on 22 November 1439 (X kal. Decembris)
Raynaldus's narrative puts the Armenians' acceptance of the formula in a public session of 10 December (IV id. Decembris)
The Armenian envoys accepted in their own name, their patriarch's and all Armenians'
The catholicos's mandate in Raynaldus names Sargis and Joachim as envoys
Issaverdens says the catholicos Constantine sent four vardapets who accepted and signed the union
Andrew, abbot of Saint Antony's, envoy of the Coptic patriarch John, was heard on 31 August 1441 (Andrea da Santa Croce in Raynaldus). The friar Albert had carried the pope's letters
Cantate Domino rejoices that before three years had passed three great nations had been joined, and Andrew accepted it for Patriarch John and his people
Mansi dates Cantate Domino to 4 February 1442, the year 1441 in Florentine reckoning
Denzinger and Mirbt print Cantate Domino as of 4 February 1441
Eugenius's letter calls Andrew and Peter the deacon envoys of Constantine, emperor of the Ethiopians, or Prester John
Dillmann, as Perruchon reports, says the monks were sent by Nicodemus, head of the Ethiopian convent in Jerusalem, without the king's or patriarch's knowledge
Perruchon says the Ethiopian chronicles say nothing of the embassy to Florence
Patrizi puts in April 1442 the session at Florence that moved the council to Rome
Mansi argues that session belongs to 1441
In a Lateran session on 30 September 1444 Abdallah, archbishop of Edessa, accepted the faith for Ignatius, patriarch of the Syrians. The decree says he had read the Florentine decrees in Arabic

Timothy, metropolitan of the Chaldeans of Cyprus, and Isaac for Elias, bishop of the Maronites, were received in a Lateran session. The bull Benedictus sit Deus, dated at St Peter's on 7 August 1445, gave them the rights of other Catholics
Denzinger's heading dates the council of Florence 1438-1445
Mansi's tomus 35 heading dates it 1438-1446, begun at Ferrara, continued at Florence and ended at Rome
Chalkokondyles says the pope made Bessarion and Isidore cardinals
Doukas says people asked the returning bishops 'Did we win?' and they answered 'We have sold our faith, we have traded piety for impiety'. Antony of Heraclea and others who signed spoke so
Doukas says some bishops would not sign until paid
Mark's letter to the faithful calls the unionists Graeco-Latins, half-beasts like the centaurs, and asks what union this is where no plain sign appears
Mark wrote to Scholarios that church affairs were never put right by middle ways: between truth and falsehood there is nothing in between
Mark wrote that the city was guarded in vain 'by the Pope's gold' and called the council the falsely named synod
Petit says the new patriarch Metrophanes proclaimed the union in the islands in June and July 1440
Mansi prints a 1443 decree of the patriarchs of Alexandria, Antioch and Jerusalem against Metrophanes and Florence. He thinks it a forgery by a Greek partisan
Mouravieff says the other patriarchs met at Constantinople and condemned the acts of Florence
Mouravieff says Mark alone did not sign, and that the emperor came home without help from any western ruler

Mouravieff says Isidore had the acts proclaimed in the Dormition cathedral at Moscow, and Basil called him a traitor. The bishops rejected the pope as Vicar of Christ and the Filioque. Isidore escaped from the Chudov monastery
Harasiewicz says Grand Prince Basil opposed the union in Moscow and Isidore went to Rome
Mouravieff says the Russian church was without a metropolitan for eight years after Isidore, until Jonah
Leonard of Chios says the union was celebrated in Constantinople on 12 December 1452, if it was not feigned
Doukas says Gennadios, once George Scholarios, posted a warning on his cell door, and that after the union people shunned Hagia Sophia like a synagogue
The Roman editor's history says the Greeks never received this council, which they call the eighth, apart from those who sat in it

The Greek chronicle printed by Bekker calls Florence the eighth synod. It came to no good end because the bishop of Ephesus refused to sign and many quarreled again at home. For that reason no help was sent
The chronicle printed by Bekker is the Historia politica of Constantinople, 1391 to 1578, printed with the patriarchal history

contested_claims.claim: How Joseph II greeted the pope at Ferrara
contested_claims.sides: He refused the foot-kiss and was received in the pope's chamber before the cardinals alone: Syropoulos (syropoulos_vera-historia-unionis-non-verae-grc-lat_creyghton1660.txt l.17860-17975). He kissed the standing pope's cheek, with no quarrel told: the Greek acts (mansi_sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-tomus-31-concilium-florentinum-lat_welter-facsimile1906.txt l.46748-46758).

contested_claims.claim: Who among the Greeks refused or avoided signing
contested_claims.sides: Mark alone: Doukas (doukas_historia-byzantina-grc-lat_bekker1834.txt l.12033-12036). Mouravieff, 1838 (mouravieff_history-of-the-church-of-russia_blackmore1842.txt l.3834). Mark refused, Isaias of Stauropolis slipped away, and neither Georgian envoy signed: Syropoulos (syropoulos_vera-historia-unionis-non-verae-grc-lat_creyghton1660.txt l.47668-47681; syropoulos_vera-historia-unionis-non-verae-grc-lat_creyghton1660.txt l.44060-44072). The printed list has no signature for Stauropolis (mansi_sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-tomus-31-concilium-florentinum-lat_welter-facsimile1906.txt l.96984-97420).

contested_claims.claim: The day Patriarch Joseph II died
contested_claims.sides: 9 June 1439: the Greek acts (mansi_sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-tomus-31-concilium-florentinum-lat_welter-facsimile1906.txt l.94680-94684). 10 June: Syropoulos (syropoulos_vera-historia-unionis-non-verae-grc-lat_creyghton1660.txt l.45238-45240) and the notes to Doukas (doukas_historia-byzantina-grc-lat_bekker1834.txt l.32658-32662).

contested_claims.claim: Whether Joseph died before or after the union
contested_claims.sides: After the union: Doukas (doukas_historia-byzantina-grc-lat_bekker1834.txt l.12087-12088). Before the signing: Syropoulos (syropoulos_vera-historia-unionis-non-verae-grc-lat_creyghton1660.txt l.45229-45232) and the notes to Doukas (doukas_historia-byzantina-grc-lat_bekker1834.txt l.32658-32664).

contested_claims.claim: The date of the bull moving the council to Ferrara
contested_claims.sides: 18 September 1437 (XIV kal. Octobris): Raynaldus (raynaldus_annales-ecclesiastici-tomus28-1424-1453-lat_theiner1874.txt l.33182-33184) and Mansi (raynaldus_annales-ecclesiastici-tomus28-1424-1453-lat_theiner1874.txt l.31586-31596). 1 October (kal. Octobris): the acts printed by Justiniani, as Mansi reports them (raynaldus_annales-ecclesiastici-tomus28-1424-1453-lat_theiner1874.txt l.31589-31592).

contested_claims.claim: The weekday of the solemn opening with the Greeks, 9 April 1438
contested_claims.sides: Wednesday of Holy Week: the Greek acts (mansi_sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-tomus-31-concilium-florentinum-lat_welter-facsimile1906.txt l.46856-46860). Tuesday of Holy Week: Petit (patrologia-orientalis-tomus15_petit-documents-concile-de-florence-purgatoire-grc-fra_graffin-nau1927.txt l.304).

contested_claims.claim: Who wrote the Greek acts
contested_claims.sides: Dorotheos of Mitylene, in Petit's brackets (patrologia-orientalis-tomus15_petit-documents-concile-de-florence-purgatoire-grc-fra_graffin-nau1927.txt l.325-327). Mansi and the file give no author (mansi_sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-tomus-31-concilium-florentinum-lat_welter-facsimile1906.txt l.46705-46718).

contested_claims.claim: The count at Basel's deposition session
contested_claims.sides: Seven bishops only: Raynaldus (raynaldus_annales-ecclesiastici-tomus28-1424-1453-lat_theiner1874.txt l.42626-42628). Aeneas Silvius, as Raynaldus quotes him: no Spanish or Aragonese prelate, and from Italy only the bishop of Grosseto and an abbot. Twenty were borrowed from two other nations (raynaldus_annales-ecclesiastici-tomus28-1424-1453-lat_theiner1874.txt l.42118-42131). Both come through the papal side. No count from Basel is held.

contested_claims.claim: The year the council moved to Rome
contested_claims.sides: April 1442: Patrizi, quoted by Raynaldus (raynaldus_annales-ecclesiastici-tomus28-1424-1453-lat_theiner1874.txt l.51816-51840). 1441: Mansi (raynaldus_annales-ecclesiastici-tomus28-1424-1453-lat_theiner1874.txt l.49284-49302).

contested_claims.claim: When the council ended
contested_claims.sides: 1445: Denzinger's heading (denzinger_enchiridion-symbolorum-lat_bannwart1911.txt l.16425-16426). 1446: Mansi's tomus 35 heading (mansi_sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-tomus-35-1414-1724-lat_welter-facsimile1902.txt l.185-187). No held act names a closing session.

contested_claims.claim: The date of the Armenian decree
contested_claims.sides: 22 November 1439: the decree's own dating clause (mansi_sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-tomus-31-concilium-florentinum-lat_welter-facsimile1906.txt l.99090-99098; raynaldus_annales-ecclesiastici-tomus28-1424-1453-lat_theiner1874.txt l.52410-52416). 10 December: Raynaldus's narrative of the session (raynaldus_annales-ecclesiastici-tomus28-1424-1453-lat_theiner1874.txt l.39768-39771).

contested_claims.claim: The year of the Coptic decree Cantate Domino
contested_claims.sides: 4 February 1441: Denzinger and Mirbt, by the Florentine year (denzinger_enchiridion-symbolorum-lat_bannwart1911.txt l.16804; mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.14485). 4 February 1442: Mansi, by modern reckoning (raynaldus_annales-ecclesiastici-tomus28-1424-1453-lat_theiner1874.txt l.49305-49311). The day agrees. Only the year-count differs.

contested_claims.claim: How many Armenian envoys came
contested_claims.sides: Four vardapets: Issaverdens (issaverdens_armenia-and-the-armenians-v2-ecclesiastical-history_1875.txt l.7338-7353). Two named in the catholicos's mandate, Sargis and Joachim: Raynaldus (raynaldus_annales-ecclesiastici-tomus28-1424-1453-lat_theiner1874.txt l.39748-39756). A mandate and a party need not match.

contested_claims.claim: The Georgian party
contested_claims.sides: Two bishops and an envoy: Syropoulos (syropoulos_vera-historia-unionis-non-verae-grc-lat_creyghton1660.txt l.9398-9404). One bishop and one lay prince: Syropoulos later (syropoulos_vera-historia-unionis-non-verae-grc-lat_creyghton1660.txt l.43930-43938).

contested_claims.claim: Who sent the Ethiopian envoys
contested_claims.sides: The emperor, called Constantine: Eugenius's letter (raynaldus_annales-ecclesiastici-tomus28-1424-1453-lat_theiner1874.txt l.49240-49247). Zara Yaqob: Patrizi, as Mansi reports (raynaldus_annales-ecclesiastici-tomus28-1424-1453-lat_theiner1874.txt l.49290-49296; raynaldus_annales-ecclesiastici-tomus28-1424-1453-lat_theiner1874.txt l.51822-51826). Nicodemus, head of the Ethiopian convent in Jerusalem, without the king's knowledge: Dillmann, as Perruchon reports (zara-yaqob_chroniques-zara-yaeqob-baeda-maryam-gez-fra_perruchon1893.txt l.578-582).

contested_claims.claim: The 1443 synod of the eastern patriarchs against Florence
contested_claims.sides: Printed by Mansi, who thinks it forged by a Greek partisan, since Sphrantzes and others do not mention it (mansi_sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-tomus-35-1414-1724-lat_welter-facsimile1902.txt l.6060-6082). Told as fact by Mouravieff, 1838 (mouravieff_history-of-the-church-of-russia_blackmore1842.txt l.3834-3838).

contested_claims.claim: Whether money bought the Greek signatures
contested_claims.sides: Some archbishops would not sign until paid: Doukas, hostile (doukas_historia-byzantina-grc-lat_bekker1834.txt l.12144-12148). Mark says they were lured by promises and gifts (john-ephesus_lives-eastern-saints-po17_brooks1923.txt l.38155-38160). No money was asked or promised at the signing: Syropoulos (syropoulos_vera-historia-unionis-non-verae-grc-lat_creyghton1660.txt l.47648-47656).

contested_claims.claim: Why the Greeks came: union in exchange for military help
contested_claims.sides: A witness's view, not a term of any decree. The city guarded by the Pope's gold: Mark (gennadius-scholarius_opera-omnia-pg160-grc-lat_migne1866.txt l.99660-99666). No help sent afterwards: the Greek chronicle printed by Bekker (historia-politica-et-patriarchica-constantinopoleos_grc-lat_bekker1849.txt l.539-541). No western ruler helped: Mouravieff (mouravieff_history-of-the-church-of-russia_blackmore1842.txt l.3838-3843). Turkish pressure: the Roman history (mansi_sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-tomus-31-concilium-florentinum-lat_welter-facsimile1906.txt l.45847-45852). Manuel II's advice: the chronicle under Sphrantzes's name (sphrantzes-cananus-anagnostes_chronicles-grc-lat_bekker1838.txt l.10236-10242). The decree states no bargain (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.14262-14300).

contested_claims.claim: Whether Basel remained a council after the transfer
contested_claims.sides: No: Glassberger's editors (glassberger_chronica-analecta-franciscana-v2-lat_1887.txt l.21233-21238). The Fifth Lateran Council (mirbt_quellen-zur-geschichte-des-papsttums-3e-aufl-deu-lat_1911.txt l.15132-15140). Ferrara's decree (raynaldus_annales-ecclesiastici-tomus28-1424-1453-lat_theiner1874.txt l.35524-35538). Yes: the Lausanne synod's decree (mansi_sacrorum-conciliorum-collectio-tomus-32-1438-1549-lat_welter-facsimile1901.txt l.6988-6996). Eugenius in 1446 received Basel up to the transfer (denzinger_enchiridion-symbolorum-lat_bannwart1911.txt l.16216-16221).

contested_claims.claim: The force of Basel's Immaculate Conception definition
contested_claims.sides: Defined by Basel in session (glassberger_chronica-analecta-franciscana-v2-lat_1887.txt l.21183-21185). Never binding, since not the act of a lawful council: Glassberger's Quaracchi editors (glassberger_chronica-analecta-franciscana-v2-lat_1887.txt l.21233-21238).

absent_details.detail: Basel's session acts (Mansi, tomi 29 and 30)
absent_details.note: Not held. Searched the Library for Mansi tomi (29 and 30 absent) and grepped all texts for Basel council phrases. Basel reaches us only in quotation (Raynaldus, Glassberger, Mirbt's Pragmatic Sanction, Mansi 31 appendices and Mansi 32's Lausanne decrees).

absent_details.detail: A roll of Basel's members at any time
absent_details.note: Not held. The only counts are Mansi's note on the opening and Raynaldus's and Aeneas's on the deposition session.

absent_details.detail: Syropoulos on the patriarch's note being written for him
absent_details.note: No held line. The dossier searched Syropoulos's Latin around l.44000-48500 for terms for a note, will or writing, and read the death passage l.45180-45252. Nothing found. The Greek is garbled and was not searched.

absent_details.detail: The day of Basel's suspension of Eugenius (session XXXI)
absent_details.note: Not in a held line. Glassberger names the session without a day (glassberger l.21065-21068).

absent_details.detail: Felix V's election day from a second witness
absent_details.note: Only Glassberger gives 17 November 1439. Searched Raynaldus 1439-1440 for Novemb/Octob, Mansi 31 l.1-45700 for Amedeus, Savoy and Novembr, and Mansi 32 l.5800-7200. None gives the day.

absent_details.detail: A Coptic-side witness to the union of 1442
absent_details.note: Renaudot's history of the Coptic patriarchs was searched for Eugenius, Florence, Andrew the abbot and the years 1439-1442. Nothing on Florence. Only Roman texts hold it.

absent_details.detail: An Ethiopian-side witness
absent_details.note: Perruchon says the chronicles of Zara Yaqob say nothing of Florence (zara-yaqob l.668-675). Ludolf's works mention Florence but were not read in context.

absent_details.detail: An Armenian text of 1439
absent_details.note: Not held. The Armenian envoys' address is held only in Latin (Mansi 35). Chamich has one line and Issaverdens a short account.

absent_details.detail: A Russian text of the time on the rejection
absent_details.note: Not held. The rejection rests on Mouravieff (1838, English 1842) and Harasiewicz (1862).

absent_details.detail: The Armenian envoys' names in the decree
absent_details.note: Searched Mansi 31 for Armen. The decree does not name them. Raynaldus names two from the catholicos's mandate.

absent_details.detail: Bernardino of Siena or John of Capistrano at the council
absent_details.note: No held line puts either at Ferrara or Florence (searched Glassberger l.20985-21250). Raynaldus quotes Capistrano's tract against the deposition, but his attendance is not shown.

absent_details.detail: The day the Greeks reached Constantinople on their return
absent_details.note: The notes to Doukas give 1 February, but the year digits are garbled in our copy (doukas l.32665-32667). Not given in the entry.
